open_questions: Why stellar density from transit (fit_log_density_ratio -2.88, density_penalty 601.2) is inconsistent with TIC M-dwarf radius 0.554 Rsun - requires longer-baseline light curve or spectroscopy to verify radius/spot treatment

Odd-even depth difference diff_sigma 3.585 (odd 373 ppm vs even 640 ppm) at 3.6 sigma with depth_ratio 1.7 - marginal, not confirmed in individual sectors (max 2.862, 0 sectors over 3), but merits continued monitoring

Why transit depths vary from 465 to 777 ppm across SPOC sectors - likely spot/detrending given 15084-19678 ppm spot amplitudes vs 487 ppm dip, but higher-precision photometry would test spot-induced depth changes
dossier.public_summary: A 1.4 Earth-radius, flat-bottomed 2.5-hour dip repeats every 3.26 days on the target M dwarf, seen in 29 transits and confirmed on-sky by difference imaging. Depth jumps between early and late TESS sectors reflect pipeline differences and strong stellar spots (period matches the 3.27-day dip by chance), not a background binary. It remains the best planet explanation pending radius refinement.

reasons.why: Negative V-signal favours flat bottom over V-shaped eclipse; supports transit shape despite high impact parameter (fit_b 0.9717).
difference imaging in 3 sectors puts dip on target (offset 1.502 arcsec, sigma 0.8634) with all neighbours that could fake it 15.6 sigma or more away; rules out NEB.
Small size is planet-sized and undiluted depth 499 ppm consistent; below 10 Rearth giant-planet limit.

sectors p_constant 2.923e-12 is driven by QLP (68 +/-66 ppm, 2 sectors) vs SPOC 2-min (627 +/-39 ppm, 3 sectors, p_constant 0.037); not changes_within_a_source, so calibration/pipeline difference explains depth scatter, not evolving binary.
30 transits, top three carry only ~30% of signal and no outliers, so not a few bad events; inconsistent p 7.4e-09 is driven by sector/calibration offset.

Scorer low but specific tool answers - flat bottom, on_target centroid, small radius, steady SPOC depths - the features scorer cannot capture outweigh rank; similar look-alikes include a confirmed planet.
